forces.title: Softening global metal prices pressure Irish metals sector
forces.description: The Irish metals sector, including steel, is facing headwinds from softer global metal prices projected for 2025/26. This trend impacts profitability and necessitates careful purchasing decisions for businesses, even with favorable liquidity among major steel stockholders. Companies must monitor price movements and manage inventory to mitigate the negative effect on margins.
forces.source_title: July 2026 Ireland Sector Snippets

forces.title: Elevated raw material and labor costs challenge Irish metals
forces.description: The metals sector in Ireland is experiencing persistent pressure from high raw material and labor costs. This cost inflation, coupled with potentially softening metal prices, creates margin compression. Businesses need to assess their ability to pass on these increased costs without damaging customer relationships and maintain strong cash conversion and inventory discipline.
forces.source_title: July 2026 Ireland Sector Snippets

forces.title: Trade policy uncertainty impacts Irish metals sector
forces.description: International trade policies and tariffs present a significant uncertainty for the Irish metals sector. Such geopolitical factors can disrupt supply chains, influence input costs, and affect export markets, creating an unstable operating environment. Companies must remain vigilant and adapt strategies to navigate evolving trade landscapes.
forces.source_title: July 2026 Ireland Sector Snippets

forces.title: CBAM increases carbon costs for imported steel in the EU
forces.description: The EU's Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) moved out of its trial period in January 2026, directly linking carbon intensity to landed costs for imported goods, including steel. This increases carbon-related costs, which are largely passed onto buyers, impacting downstream industries like automotive and construction. Companies must systematically track, verify, and manage emissions data to mitigate these rising costs, with verified data potentially reducing CBAM costs by 30-85%.
forces.source_title: CBAM: How companies can build from compliance to value creation

forces.title: CBAM drives demand shift to lower-carbon steel production
forces.description: The implementation of CBAM is causing a shift in demand towards lower-carbon steel producers. As carbon intensity directly affects costs for EU importers, downstream industries are incentivized to source steel from producers with lower embedded emissions. This structural change reinforces the need for steelmakers to invest in decarbonization and robust emissions verification to maintain competitiveness and capture new demand.
forces.source_title: CBAM: How companies can build from compliance to value creation

forces.title: Verified emissions data reduces CBAM costs for steel importers
forces.description: Companies importing steel into the EU can significantly reduce their CBAM costs by using verified emissions data instead of conservative default values. Research indicates potential savings of 30-85% per metric ton. This acts as an upside driver for steel importers who invest in robust monitoring, reporting, and verification (MRV) systems, enabling better cost control, supplier allocation, and product specification decisions.
forces.source_title: CBAM: How companies can build from compliance to value creation

forces.title: Procurement shifts towards EAF steel and higher scrap content
forces.description: Driven by CBAM and decarbonization goals, companies are actively steering demand towards lower-carbon steel supplies, such as electric arc furnace (EAF) steel and products with higher scrap content. This requires renegotiating specifications and product redesigns to reduce material intensity. Leading players are securing these scarce low-carbon inputs through supplier development and long-term offtake agreements, indicating a significant shift in steel procurement strategies.
forces.source_title: CBAM: How companies can build from compliance to value creation

forces.title: Global crude steel overcapacity pressures industry margins
forces.description: In 2024, the global steel industry possessed a production capacity of over 2.5 billion tons, significantly exceeding the demand of approximately 1.9 billion tons. This persistent overcapacity, largely driven by China's historical urbanization and industrialization, compresses margins for steel producers worldwide. This imbalance acts as a significant headwind, intensifying cost competition and impacting profitability across the sector.
forces.source_title: EAF steel: Beyond the blast furnace

forces.title: Europe shifts to DRI-EAF steel for smaller carbon footprint
forces.description: European countries like Germany and Sweden are increasingly adopting Electric Arc Furnace (EAF) and Direct Reduced Iron-EAF (DRI-EAF) technologies, despite BF-BOF still dominating current production. New investments, such as Salzgitter’s Salcos facility in Germany, are specifically targeting DRI-EAF-based plants due to their significantly smaller carbon footprint. This represents a gradual but decisive phase-out of traditional BF-BOF capacity driven by environmental considerations and policy.
forces.source_title: EAF steel: Beyond the blast furnace

forces.title: EU ETS carbon pricing raises BF-BOF costs, favors DRI-EAF
forces.description: The EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS) is increasing carbon costs, particularly for blast furnace-basic oxygen furnace (BF-BOF) steel production. As free allowances are phased out and the ETS comes into full force, BF-BOF production becomes more expensive. This dynamic creates a relative advantage for DRI-EAF production, which has lower emissions, and incentivizes investments in cleaner steelmaking technologies, enabling them to capture a "green" premium.
forces.source_title: EAF steel: Beyond the blast furnace

forces.title: High natural gas prices disadvantage EU DRI-EAF steel production
forces.description: European DRI-EAF steel production faces a significant cost disadvantage compared to regions with lower energy costs, such as Oman. Levelized costs in Europe are estimated to be 45-50% higher than in Oman, primarily driven by elevated natural gas prices. This economic challenge makes European DRI-EAF facilities less competitive globally unless offset by carbon pricing mechanisms, subsidies, or "green" premiums.
forces.source_title: EAF steel: Beyond the blast furnace

forces.title: Swedish and German steel face severe gas price disadvantage
forces.description: Sweden and Germany face substantial cost disadvantages in DRI-EAF steel production due to high natural gas prices. In 2024, Sweden's gas prices per ton were 4-5 times higher than Oman's, adding approximately $250 to its steel cost. Germany's gas costs were 2-3 times higher, adding about 25%. This large energy cost gap is a primary driver of higher levelized costs in European steel production.
forces.source_title: EAF steel: Beyond the blast furnace

forces.title: German steel production burdened by high electricity costs
forces.description: Germany's DRI-EAF steel production is significantly impacted by high electricity costs, which are nearly double those in Oman. This adds a markup of approximately $80 per ton (15%) to German steel, contributing to its overall higher levelized cost. Although subsidies for heavy industry may partially mitigate this for individual producers, it remains a considerable headwind for the sector's competitiveness.
forces.source_title: EAF steel: Beyond the blast furnace

forces.title: Higher labor costs in Germany and Sweden impact steel competitiveness
forces.description: Labor costs contribute an additional $20-30 per ton to steel produced in Germany and Sweden, where salaries are significantly higher than in regions like Oman. While this impact is substantially less than energy costs, it still represents a factor contributing to the higher overall production costs in these European nations, slightly eroding their competitive position in the global steel market.
forces.source_title: EAF steel: Beyond the blast furnace

forces.title: Scrap availability offers material cost advantage to German/Swedish steel
forces.description: Germany and Sweden benefit from a $20-30 per ton material cost advantage in steelmaking compared to Oman, primarily due to their larger domestic steel stock, which ensures greater availability of scrap. This local scrap supply reduces reliance on imported pellets, offering a slight competitive edge in raw material sourcing, though it is insufficient to offset the larger energy cost disparities.
forces.source_title: EAF steel: Beyond the blast furnace

forces.title: Hydrogen-powered DRI-EAF lowers Swedish steel costs, still faces global gap
forces.description: Sweden is pursuing hydrogen-powered DRI-EAF technology, leveraging low-cost hydropower, with projects like Stegra. This transition is projected to reduce Sweden's levelized steel production cost from $750 to $665 per ton. However, even with this improvement, Swedish hydrogen-powered DRI-EAF steel remains significantly more expensive—$170 more per ton than Oman's DRI-EAF and $285 more than India's BF-BOF steel—underscoring persistent global competitiveness challenges.
forces.source_title: EAF steel: Beyond the blast furnace

forces.title: Europe faces risk of energy-intensive steel production relocation
forces.description: Regions with structurally high energy costs, such as Europe, may face the relocation of energy-intensive steel production steps to areas with more abundant and cheaper energy resources, like the Middle East or the United States. For DRI-EAF production, this could mean shifting the DRI step while retaining the EAF, rolling, and finishing nearer to demand. This represents a significant long-term risk to the full value chain of European steelmaking.
forces.source_title: EAF steel: Beyond the blast furnace

forces.title: EU-27 imposes 50% tariff on steel imports exceeding quotas
forces.description: The EU-27 applies a 50% tariff on steel imports that exceed predefined quotas. This measure impacts international trade dynamics, aiming to protect the domestic steel industry from global overcapacity and potentially influence supply chain decisions for companies importing steel into Europe. While supporting local production, it increases the cost of imported steel, impacting downstream users.
forces.source_title: EAF steel: Beyond the blast furnace

forces.title: New technologies drive sustained high demand for steel
forces.description: Emerging technologies, including artificial intelligence, electric vehicles (EVs), and renewable-energy infrastructure, are acting as significant growth engines, generating sustained high demand for steel. For example, AI-driven data center investments are projected to be substantial, and these sectors require higher-quality materials with tighter tolerances. This creates a strong tailwind for the steel sector, particularly for producers capable of meeting specialized material specifications.
forces.source_title: The next wave of value in the materials supply chain

forces.title: European defense buildup boosts materials demand, including steel
forces.description: European countries are significantly increasing defense spending, with incremental outlays of €700-800 billion projected for 2022-2028, potentially reaching €500 billion annually by 2028. This modernization and ammunition replenishment drive an 18% annual growth in relevant materials categories, including steel. This robust demand from the defense sector provides a strong tailwind for steel producers and service centers, especially those offering certified materials and integrated logistics.
forces.source_title: The next wave of value in the materials supply chain

forces.title: European materials distribution and processing sector consolidates
forces.description: The structurally fragmented materials distribution and processing market in Europe, including steel, is entering a consolidation phase. This is driven by the increasing service intensity, rising costs, and more rigorous technical specifications for products. Players are seeking greater scale, deeper capabilities, and stronger competitive positioning through M&A, as evidenced by intense activity in 2025, to address market inefficiencies and capture new value pools.
forces.source_title: The next wave of value in the materials supply chain

forces.title: Middle East conflict elevates European energy costs, impacting steel
forces.description: The Middle East conflict has triggered significant energy inflation in Europe, leading to increased gas and electricity prices. This translates into higher operational costs for energy-intensive industries like steel manufacturing, eroding margins and potentially delaying investment decisions. The geopolitical instability and its direct impact on energy inputs present a considerable headwind for the European steel sector, contributing to lower growth and higher inflation.
forces.source_title: Bank of Ireland Sectors Team — Developments & Insights May 2026

forces.title: US 50% tariff on steel imports challenges Irish exports
forces.description: As part of US trade policy, a 50% tariff applies to steel and aluminum imports. While this directly impacts imports into the US, it acts as a headwind for Irish steel producers seeking to export to the US market. Despite Ireland's generally low trade-weighted average tariff, this specific tariff barrier significantly increases the cost and reduces the competitiveness of Irish steel products in the US, affecting trade flows.
forces.source_title: Bank of Ireland Sectors Team — Manufacturing Sector H2 2025 Insights and H1 2026 Outlook

forces.title: Steel prices decline year-over-year, impacting revenue
forces.description: As of January 2026, steel prices have experienced a year-over-year decline compared to January 2025. This downward movement in prices represents a cyclical headwind for steel producers, potentially impacting revenue and profitability, even as other manufacturing inputs remain elevated above pre-Covid levels. Companies must manage pricing strategies and cost structures to mitigate the effects of this price softening.
forces.source_title: Bank of Ireland Sectors Team — Manufacturing Sector H2 2025 Insights and H1 2026 Outlook

forces.title: Timber construction emerges as steel substitution risk
forces.description: The promotion of timber in construction, particularly as part of Ireland's Forest Strategy 2023-2030, presents a key risk to the steel sector. Timber is positioned as a sustainable, home-grown alternative that can replace steel and concrete, reducing the carbon footprint of buildings. This trend highlights a potential shift in material preferences for construction projects, posing a competitive threat through substitution for conventional steel products.
forces.source_title: Situation and Outlook for Irish Agriculture 2026

forces.title: Steel prices exhibit high volatility in competitive markets
forces.description: Unlike building materials such as concrete and cement, steel is traded in more competitive international markets, leading to significantly higher price volatility. This "bumpier road" in steel prices poses a key risk for steel producers and downstream users, making financial forecasting and margin management more challenging. Companies must develop robust strategies to navigate these frequent price fluctuations.
forces.source_title: The worst is over for Europe's building materials industry

forces.title: US metals tariffs risk trade diversion, affecting EU metal prices
forces.description: US tariffs on metals, including steel, could lead to trade diversion, where products originally destined for the US market are redirected to other regions, including the EU. This influx of diverted supply could directly impact local EU metal prices, potentially driving them down and creating a headwind for European steel producers. This risk highlights the interconnectedness of global trade policies.
forces.source_title: The worst is over for Europe's building materials industry

forces.title: Steel prices fall due to weak demand and China's overcapacity
forces.description: Steel prices witnessed a 16% year-over-year decline in January 2025, driven primarily by lower demand globally and persistent overcapacity from China. The collapse of China's construction sector has freed up significant production capacity, exacerbating the supply-demand imbalance. This downward pressure on prices poses a substantial headwind for European steel producers, impacting their profitability and market stability.
forces.source_title: Bank of Ireland Manufacturing 2024 Insights and 2025 Outlook February 2025

viewpoints.title: Irish metals sector faces headwinds despite construction link and stable conditions
viewpoints.description: The metals sector in Ireland, closely tied to construction, engineering, manufacturing, and agri-business, is experiencing moderate demand from ongoing project activity. However, it faces headwinds in 2025/26 from softening global metal prices, persistent raw material and labor cost pressures, and trade policy uncertainty. Despite these challenges, the sector shows resilience with stable trading conditions and low insolvency levels among steel stockholders, suggesting cautious optimism.

viewpoints.title: European green steel investments dependent on policy support and carbon pricing
viewpoints.description: Investments in DRI-EAF or hydrogen-powered DRI-EAF steel production in Europe are primarily policy-dependent. Their viability relies on rising carbon prices, the phasing out of free allowances under EU ETS, or the securing of equivalent subsidies and "green" premium support. This contrasts with cost-driven investments in BF-BOF in Asia. Europe's strategic shift towards lower-emissions steel is progressing, but its economic competitiveness remains contingent on robust policy frameworks and market incentives.
viewpoints.source_title: EAF steel: Beyond the blast furnace

demand_drivers.description: Increased carbon costs incentivize sourcing of lower-carbon steel.
Corporate commitments to reduce emissions drive demand for sustainable steel products.

pnl_drivers.description: Linking product prices to CBAM costs and verified emissions outcomes to protect margins.
Aligning contracts with carbon price references to manage cost volatility.
Using EUA-linked instruments to stabilize average cost levels for imported steel.

new_opportunities.description: Opportunity for steelmakers to offer EAF steel, higher scrap content products, or certified low-carbon production routes to meet evolving demand.
Developing capabilities to track, verify, and manage emissions data for competitive advantage and cost reduction under CBAM.

market_sizing.methodology: Analysis of procurement strategies shifting demand towards lower-carbon steel, specifically EAF steel and higher scrap content. Companies are renegotiating specifications, redesigning products for material intensity reduction (light-weighting, yield improvements, substitution), and securing low-carbon inputs through long-term agreements.
market_sizing.source_title: CBAM: How companies can build from compliance to value creation

demand_drivers.description: Increased costs for BF-BOF production under EU ETS make DRI-EAF more attractive.
Opportunity to capture higher prices for lower-carbon steel products.
Government incentives for decarbonization drive investment in new technologies like hydrogen-powered DRI-EAF.

market_sizing.methodology: Plans are underway for more than 17 EAF and DRI-EAF steel plants in Europe, specifically projected to produce roughly 40 to 50 million tons of low-carbon steel. This reflects investment driven by policy support and carbon pricing incentives.
market_sizing.source_title: EAF steel: Beyond the blast furnace

demand_drivers.description: Reorganization of supply chains and reshoring of industrial processes are driving domestic materials demand.
Buyers' plans to increase the share of green metals (e.g., steel) from 21% today to 32% by 2030.
Demand from data centers, electric vehicles, and renewable-energy infrastructure.
Manufacturers increasingly outsourcing processing and logistics to wholesalers/service centers.

market_sizing.methodology: Following a period of marginal change from 2015-2024, total consumption of steel, aluminum, copper, and stainless steel in Europe is expected to accelerate and return to sustained growth by 2030. This growth is driven by geopolitical realignment, decarbonization, new technologies, and outsourcing trends.
market_sizing.source_title: The next wave of value in the materials supply chain

demand_drivers.description: Increasing need for reliable material sourcing amidst geopolitical tensions and trade fragmentation.
Demand for mechanisms to mitigate fluctuating material prices.
Customers seeking diversified sourcing options beyond direct mill relationships.

market_sizing.methodology: The global raw and semifinished-materials trading market, which includes steel, was estimated to be between €300 billion and €400 billion in 2024. This market is projected to grow at a 3-4% CAGR through 2030.
market_sizing.source_title: The next wave of value in the materials supply chain

new_opportunities.description: Evolving from materials provision to offering kitting, light assembly, and integrated logistics services to capture higher margins downstream.
Exploiting market fragmentation through strategic M&A to build local scale and presence, enabling faster delivery and stronger customer relationships.

market_sizing.methodology: The metals service market in Europe is structurally fragmented, characterized by a highly distributed market share among numerous regional and midsize service centers and niche specialists, with even the largest players holding modest shares. This fragmentation creates inefficiencies in capacity utilization and technology investment, driving a trend towards consolidation as players seek scale and deeper capabilities.
market_sizing.source_title: The next wave of value in the materials supply chain

demand_drivers.description: Continued operation of blast furnace-basic oxygen furnace (BF-BOF) steelmaking relies on metallurgical coal.

market_sizing.methodology: Global demand for metallurgical coal, a crucial input for industrial iron and steel production, is projected to persist into the longer term. This indicates a continued reliance on this raw material for conventional steelmaking processes, especially in regions where BF-BOF technology remains dominant.
